newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain, China at odds on HK handover guest list.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China at odds on HK handover guest list.

text.p: Britain and China failed on Friday to agree on a guest list for the historic ceremony marking Hong Kong's return to Beijing's control this year.
British and Chinese negotiators came away from their latest diplomatic talks with no deal on the names of the 4,000 guests who will attend the handover party on the night of June 30.
Lu Ping, China's Hong Kong policy chief, meanwhile, prepared to launch a last-ditch effort to convince the world that Hong Kong has a bright future under Chinese rule.

Hugh Davies, Britain's chief negotiator, said after more than three hours of talks that the final guest list had not been agreed, making it unlikely the list could be ready for next week's full meeting of the Joint Liaison Group in London.
"I don't think we will reach agreement next week but we will go on working in the next few weeks... we are still exploring the general outline of the meeting," Davies told reporters.
One sticking point apparently was how to include a representative from Taiwan, which China also wants eventually to reunify with the mainland.

"I'm sure there will be representatives from Taiwan," Davies said when asked whether Taiwan representatives would be invited. Before the session, Davies was optimistic an agreement would be reached on VIP guests before next Tuesday's London meeting, the second to last before China takes over Hong Kong.
Davies' Chinese counterpart Zhao Jihua confirmed that an agreement on the issue was not imminent. Zhao dodged the issue of Taiwan. "This is a question we need to consider," he said.

Lu Ping, who heads up Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, will visit Europe and Canada later this month to try to assure government and business circles about the territory's future as part of China, a pro-China newspaper said.
Lu would visit Germany and Austria between March 16 and 26, the Beijing-controlled daily Wen Wei Pao said.
In April he would go to other European countries and Canada, which has a large number of Hong Kong Chinese who emigrated in recent years out of fears over Beijing's control of Hong Kong.
China had sought to reverse the negative image it has earned abroad as a result of its plans to roll back civil liberties and democracy in Hong Kong, a political analyst said.
"It's vital in April, May, June and July. They have got to get on top of the information flow to change people's perceptions," Michael DeGolyer of Hong Kong Baptist University told Reuters.
Lu will try to assure governments and businessmen Hong Kong would enjoy a high degree of self-rule after the handover.

Under the Sino-British handover treaty, Hong Kong has been promised a large degree of autonomy and the continuation of its capitalist way of life under a "one country, two systems" formula for the next 50 years.
